_source: Offline reference of general patient-education facts. Describes what tests mean and known medicine effects on lab values. Contains NO treatment, drug or dosing advice.

hemoglobin.what: The protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen.
hemoglobin.low: Anemia. Common causes: iron deficiency, blood loss (including heavy periods), low B12 or folate, chronic disease.
hemoglobin.high: Dehydration, smoking, living at high altitude, or lung/heart conditions.
hemoglobin.next: Often checked together with ferritin, iron studies, B12 and folate.

hematocrit.what: The percentage of your blood made up of red blood cells.
hematocrit.low: Usually moves with hemoglobin; suggests anemia.
hematocrit.high: Dehydration or conditions that raise red cell production.

mcv.what: The average size of your red blood cells.
mcv.low: Small red cells (microcytosis), most commonly from iron deficiency; also thalassemia trait.
mcv.high: Large red cells, often from low B12 or folate, alcohol use, or some medicines.

white blood cells.low: Viral infections, some medicines, or bone marrow problems.
white blood cells.high: Infection, inflammation, stress, steroids, or rarely blood disorders.

platelets.what: Cell fragments that help blood clot.
platelets.low: Bleeding risk rises when very low; causes include viral infections, medicines, liver disease.
platelets.high: Inflammation, iron deficiency, or after surgery.

ferritin.what: A protein that stores iron; the best single test of your iron stores.
ferritin.low: Low iron stores (iron deficiency), even before anemia appears. Common causes: heavy periods, low dietary iron, poor absorption, blood loss from the gut.
ferritin.high: Inflammation, liver disease, or iron overload.
ferritin.next: Your doctor can look into the cause of low iron stores.

glucose.what: The sugar level in your blood. Fasting means no food for 8+ hours.
glucose.high: Fasting 100-125 mg/dL is in the prediabetes range; 126+ on two tests suggests diabetes.
glucose.low: Below 70 mg/dL can cause shakiness, sweating and confusion.

hemoglobin a1c.what: Your average blood sugar over the last 2-3 months.
hemoglobin a1c.high: 5.7-6.4% is the prediabetes range; 6.5% or higher suggests diabetes.
hemoglobin a1c.next: Your doctor will interpret this together with your fasting glucose and health history.

alt.what: A liver enzyme. When liver cells are irritated or damaged, ALT leaks into the blood.
alt.high: Fatty liver (common with high sugar or cholesterol), alcohol, viral hepatitis, or medicines such as statins or acetaminophen.
alt.next: Often rechecked, sometimes with a liver ultrasound.

creatinine.what: A waste product filtered by the kidneys; used to estimate kidney function.
creatinine.high: Reduced kidney function, dehydration, or high muscle mass.
creatinine.low: Low muscle mass; usually not a concern.

sodium.what: A salt that controls fluid balance and nerve function.
sodium.low: Too much water, some medicines (like diuretics), or hormone problems.

potassium.what: A mineral important for heart rhythm and muscles.
potassium.high: Kidney problems, some blood pressure medicines; can affect heart rhythm.

total cholesterol.what: All the cholesterol in your blood.
total cholesterol.high: Raises long-term risk of heart disease and stroke, especially with high LDL.

ldl cholesterol.what: 'Bad' cholesterol that can build up in artery walls.
ldl cholesterol.high: Linked to higher long-term risk of heart attack and stroke.
ldl cholesterol.next: Doctors weigh LDL with your overall heart risk (age, blood pressure, smoking, diabetes).

hdl cholesterol.what: 'Good' cholesterol that helps clear other cholesterol.
hdl cholesterol.low: Below 40 mg/dL is linked to higher heart risk.

triglycerides.what: A type of fat in the blood, affected by recent meals, sugar and alcohol.
triglycerides.high: Linked to heart risk and prediabetes. Can be affected by recent meals, sugar and alcohol.

tsh.what: A hormone that tells your thyroid how hard to work.

vitamin d.what: A vitamin important for bones, muscles and immunity.
vitamin d.low: Common, especially with little sun exposure. Below 20 ng/mL is usually called deficient.
vitamin d.next: Your doctor will decide whether anything needs to be done and when to recheck.

affects.alt: Statins can raise liver enzymes (ALT). Usually mild, but doctors monitor it.

affects.mcv: Long-term metformin can lower vitamin B12, which can change red cell size.
affects.hemoglobin: Low B12 from metformin can contribute to anemia.

affects.alt: High doses, or use with alcohol, can raise ALT.

affects.creatinine: Regular NSAID use can strain the kidneys and raise creatinine.
affects.hemoglobin: NSAIDs can cause stomach bleeding, which can lower hemoglobin and ferritin.
affects.ferritin: Hidden stomach bleeding from NSAIDs can lower iron stores.
Long-term PPIs reduce stomach acid, which can lower iron absorption.
affects.hemoglobin: Reduced iron and B12 absorption can contribute to anemia.

affects.tsh: The dose directly changes TSH; it is used to adjust the dose.

affects.white blood cells: Steroids raise the white blood cell count.
